Polybutylene Pipes in Florida Homes: Risks and Replacement

By SRQ Leak Pros Editorial · Published November 4, 2026 · Updated November 7, 2026 · 5 min read

Short answer: Polybutylene pipes are gray, sometimes blue or black, plastic water pipes used in several million U.S. and Canadian homes from about 1978 to 1997. They can break down in chlorinated water and leak at fittings, which led to a $1 billion class action settlement. They're no longer accepted by U.S. building codes. Many Florida owners choose to repipe.

If your Florida home was built or replumbed between the late 1970s and the late 1990s, it may have polybutylene pipe. Many homes with it have never had a problem. But the material has a known history, and some insurers ask about it. If you find it, SRQ Leak Pros can connect you with a local pro for repiping in Sarasota.

What are polybutylene pipes?

Polybutylene, often called "poly-B," is a plastic resin used for water supply pipe. According to Wikipedia, it was used in several million homes in the United States and Canada from around 1978 to 1997. It was cheap and easy to install, which made it popular in fast-growing areas.

How to tell if you have polybutylene pipes

  • Gray plastic pipe, sometimes blue or black
  • A printed stamp on the pipe that includes the letters "PB"
  • Pipe coming out of walls to sinks and toilets
  • Pipe at the water heater
  • Gray plastic where the service line enters the house
  • Plastic or copper crimp fittings joining sections

Check under sinks, at the water heater, in the attic and where the main line enters the house. A pro can confirm it during a visit.

Why polybutylene pipes fail

Wikipedia explains that chlorine and chloramine compounds in municipal water can break down polybutylene and its acetal fittings. The damage speeds up under stress, so it is most often seen at fittings, sharp bends and kinks. In extreme cases, leaks can start within a few years. Failures may come with little warning.

Weak pointWhat happens
FittingsCracks and splits where pipe joins
Bends and kinksStress whitening, then cracking
Hot water linesHeat adds stress
Exposed sectionsSunlight can weaken plastic

The class action and building codes

Problems with leaks and broken pipes led to a class action lawsuit, Cox v. Shell Oil, that Wikipedia reports was settled for $1 billion. Polybutylene water pipe is no longer accepted by U.S. building codes. Claim deadlines for that settlement have long passed, so owners today pay for replacement themselves or through insurance where it applies.

Polybutylene and home insurance in Florida

Some insurers ask about pipe type when writing or renewing a policy, and some may decline or surcharge homes with polybutylene. If you have a leak, your policy may cover sudden water damage but not the pipe itself. Florida Statutes § 627.70132 requires notice of a property insurance claim within 1 year after the date of loss. Ask your agent how your pipe affects coverage. This is general information, not insurance advice.

Should you replace polybutylene pipes?

Many owners choose to replace it before it fails. Consider a repipe if:

  • You've had any leak in the system
  • You're selling, buying or refinancing and it came up in an inspection
  • Your insurer has raised it
  • You're planning a remodel that opens walls
  • The home sits empty part of the year

What replaces polybutylene?

MaterialNotes
PEXFlexible cross-linked polyethylene; common for repipes
CopperLong track record; costs more
CPVCRigid plastic used for hot and cold lines

Wikipedia notes that PEX is used mainly for building pipework and domestic water piping. A repipe usually runs new lines through the attic and walls, which also avoids future slab leaks.

The service line may be polybutylene too

Polybutylene was used for some buried service lines as well. If your yard line is gray plastic at the meter or the house entry, ask about a water line replacement at the same time as the repipe.

Buying or selling a home with polybutylene

Home inspectors often note polybutylene in their reports. If you're buying, ask the seller whether the pipe has leaked and whether any of it has been replaced. Get a repipe quote before closing so you know the cost. If you're selling, records of a past repipe or partial replacement can help buyers and their insurers feel more confident. Ask your real estate agent how it affects your deal.

How to lower risk until you replace

  • Keep water pressure in a normal range; ask about a pressure reducing valve.
  • Avoid kinking or stressing exposed pipe.
  • Close the main shut-off when you leave for long trips.
  • Consider leak sensors near the water heater and sinks.
  • Check exposed fittings for whitening or cracks.

Local note: many homes in North Port and Venice were built during the years polybutylene was used, so it's worth checking. Older homes in Nokomis may have been replumbed in that period.

Call a pro when:

  • You find gray PB pipe in your home
  • You've had a leak from a fitting or pipe
  • Your insurer or home inspector flags it
  • You're planning a remodel

Frequently asked questions

Are all gray plastic pipes polybutylene?

Not always. PEX can also be gray in some brands. Look for a PB stamp, or ask a pro to confirm.

Is polybutylene pipe illegal in Florida?

It is no longer accepted by U.S. building codes for new installs. Existing pipe isn't illegal to have, but many owners replace it.

Can I replace only the leaking section of polybutylene?

You can, but other fittings may fail later. Many pros recommend replacing the whole system.

How long does a polybutylene repipe take?

Many homes are repiped in a few days, depending on size and access.
